items.followUp: Define inorganic chemistry and name two industries that use it.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: Defines organic chemistry as the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both hydrocarbons and their derivatives as its subject matter.

rubric.why: Checks that industries covered by organic chemistry are named.
rubric.description: Names industries such as petroleum, pharmaceutical, polymer/plastics, food, or textile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a relevant industry.

modelAnswer: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
It covers industries such as petroleum, pharmaceuticals, polymers and plastics, and food.

items.followUp: State the modern definition of an atom.

rubric.why: The modern definition identifies an element by its nuclear proton number.
rubric.description: States that atoms of an element have the same number of protons or the same atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either equivalent statement.

rubric.why: Confirms that the definition is about the identity of an element based on its atoms.
rubric.description: Clearly identifies the substance as an element whose atoms share this property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the answer explicitly connects the shared proton number to an element.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of atoms having the same number of protons in their nuclei.
Therefore, all atoms of an element have the same atomic number.

items.followUp: Explain molecular formula and give one example.

rubric.why: This is the defining feature of an empirical formula.
rubric.description: Defines it as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the simplest whole-number ratio.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates the meaning of the formula.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, with empirical formula CH₂O.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example and its empirical formula.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
For example, glucose has the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆; its empirical formula is CH₂O.

items.followUp: Differentiate between an orbital and an energy level, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of a shell and its place in the atom.
rubric.description: States that a shell is a principal energy level around the nucleus and gives a shell example such as K, L, or n = 1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct shell description with an example.

rubric.why: Checks that subshells are subdivisions of shells and recognizes their notation.
rubric.description: States that a subshell is a subdivision of a shell and gives an example such as s, p, d, or f.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct subshell description with an example.

modelAnswer: A shell is a principal energy level around the nucleus and contains one or more subshells; shells are labelled K, L, M, or by n = 1, 2, 3.
A subshell is a subdivision of a shell; subshells are labelled s, p, d, and f.

items.followUp: Name the three naturally occurring isotopes of hydrogen and state how they differ.

rubric.why: Isotopes of uranium share the same atomic number and proton number.
rubric.description: States that uranium isotopes all have 92 protons (atomic number 92).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the shared proton number or atomic number.

rubric.why: The isotope mass numbers distinguish the uranium isotopes.
rubric.description: Names uranium-234, uranium-235, and uranium-238, which have different numbers of neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the three isotopes or their mass numbers.

modelAnswer: The naturally occurring isotopes of uranium are uranium-234, uranium-235, and uranium-238.
Each has 92 protons, but they have different numbers of neutrons: 142, 143, and 146, respectively.

items.followUp: Define atomic radius and state the approximate atomic radius of oxygen.

rubric.why: This is the standard definition of atomic radius for bonded identical atoms.
rubric.description: Defines atomic radius as half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the half-distance definition.

rubric.why: Checks the approximate value for carbon's atomic radius.
rubric.description: Gives carbon's atomic radius as approximately 77 pm (0.077 nm).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct approximate value and unit.

modelAnswer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element.
The atomic radius of carbon is approximately 77 pm, or 0.077 nm.

items.followUp: Define electronegativity and describe its trend down a group.

rubric.why: The definition refers to the attraction of bonding electrons by an atom.
rubric.description: Defines electronegativity as the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair towards itself.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing attraction of shared or bonding electrons.

rubric.why: This is the periodic trend asked for.
rubric.description: States that electronegativity increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

modelAnswer: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.
Across a period, electronegativity generally increases from left to right.

items.followUp: How many blocks are there in the modern periodic table, and what are they called?

rubric.why: Checks the number of vertical columns in the modern periodic table.
rubric.description: States that the modern periodic table has 18 groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct number of groups.

rubric.why: Checks the number of horizontal rows in the modern periodic table.
rubric.description: States that the modern periodic table has 7 periods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct number of periods.

modelAnswer: The modern periodic table has 18 groups (vertical columns).
